In a podcast called In Good Company, hosted by Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, on Wednesday, Schmidt said, "I don't know that they will get ahead, but I will tell you that…if they're six months behind, then we're already losing because their strategy is that the products are free."
Chinese AI models are often free or less expensive, potentially attracting consumers in developing economies that cannot afford costly, closed Western systems, he said. Open-weight models could further accelerate global use.
He credited China's progress partly to access to advanced chips he said were "not supposed to have" and were "pilfered or smuggled" into the country. He also cited distillation, in which developers query Western AI systems and train their own models using the responses.
Schmidt, who personally owns a stake in Anthropic, rejected comparisons between the AI industry and a speculative bubble. "That's real growth. It's not fake. It's real money, with real customers who are paying for something useful," he said.

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month target for South Korea's Kospi Index by 25%, citing mounting concerns over artificial intelligence investments and more conservative equity valuations.
Strategists led by Timothy Moe lowered their target to 9,000 from 12,000 after the benchmark plunged more than 35% from its June peak.
Despite the downgrade, the revised forecast still implies upside of more than 60% from current levels, reflecting the bank's view that Korean equities have become significantly undervalued.
The investment bank had previously raised its Kospi target in June and maintained its bullish outlook even as global technology stocks began retreating amid concerns about AI spending.
South Korea's market has been particularly vulnerable because of its heavy exposure to semiconductor manufacturers Samsung Electronics (KRX:005930) and SK Hynix (KRX:000660).
Both companies have benefited from demand for memory chips used in AI infrastructure, making the Kospi a major indicator of investor sentiment toward the technology.
However, concerns about rising financing costs, massive infrastructure investments and uncertain returns have triggered widespread selling across Korean equities.
Goldman's strategists said the market was pricing in an excessively pessimistic outlook for corporate fundamentals.
The Kospi's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to approximately four, a level not seen across 18 major markets since 2006.
Korean stocks now trade at roughly half the valuation of Indonesian equities, highlighting the scale of the recent selloff.
According to the bank's estimates, current semiconductor valuations imply a 65% decline in sector earnings in 2027, a scenario the strategists consider overly pessimistic.
Meanwhile, companies outside the memory chip sector, representing approximately half the Kospi, trade at 7.6 times forward earnings.
Despite lowering its overall market target, Goldman continues to favour opportunities in power, industrials, corporate governance-related stocks, and companies benefiting from domestic economic recovery and Korean popular culture.

They open eight browser tabs, one for each of the primary platforms: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, xAI, Meta, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. The goal is simple — find a per-seat or per-unit price to drop into a spreadsheet. By the time they reach the end of the list, no single metric has appeared that lets them compare one agent against another. What they have instead is a row of quote-gated portals, usage meters and third-party estimates: enough material to fill the spreadsheet, not enough to defend it.
Four of the eight publish no public enterprise-agent price on their own surface. OpenAI Presence lists no price on its product page or its announcement; the service is not self-serve, is limited to eligible enterprise customers, and routes buyers to contact sales or an account team — a quote-gated enterprise SKU, where the pricing mechanism exists and simply is not shown. Meta's Business Agent announcement says getting started is free and that paid subscription offerings are planned, but publishes no seat or subscription price. A typical marathon-training schedule involves several months of increasing mileage. But the physical gains you earn from all of those runs are only part of the equation that can make or break your race.
“As a coach, I always emphasize the importance of preparing for more than just the distance,” says Gab Reznik, NASM-certified personal trainer, run coach, and head coach at Tone House, a fitness studio in New York City. “Marathon training isn’t simply about building the fitness to cover 26.2 miles. It’s about developing the confidence, adaptability, and mental resilience to handle whatever challenges arise along the way.” Because if there’s one guarantee in the marathon, it’s that something unexpected will come your way.
To help you prepare for any scenario that pops up during your 26.2, we tapped three run coaches for their insights about what marathoners tend to report back to them postrace—the things that surprised them, the mindsets that helped them when the miles got grueling, and what they wish they’d known sooner to make the race go smoother.
Use this roundup of lessons they’ve learned along the way as your cheat sheet for a faster finish and more gratifying race day overall.
You might feel wiped out before the race even starts.
“One thing we’ve heard from several of our athletes after the marathon is how mentally exhausting the logistics of getting to the start can be; it’s a lot of hurry up and wait,” says Matt Wilpers, Peloton instructor and endurance coach. “You’re up early, navigating transportation, surrounded by thousands of other runners, and then sitting around in the athletes’ village waiting for your wave. By the time the race starts, you’ve already spent several hours managing logistics, anticipation, and nervous energy.”
This can be true regardless of your race, even if you’re not tackling one of the World Marathon Majors, but many of those races offer particularly difficult starts.
How to prep:
A little extra planning can help make all of those prerace moments feel more streamlined and less mentally taxing. Wilpers suggests treating the hours before the start as part of your race plan. “Know your transportation options, anticipate the waiting, bring food and extra layers, and eliminate as many uncertainties as possible,” he says. “The more decisions you make in advance, the more energy and attention you’ll have available when it matters most.”
Reznik also advises packing a portable charger, which is especially wise for big races, as the athletes’ village and start line at those often have bad cell service. “The last thing you want is to arrive at the starting line with a dead phone,” she says.
It’s way too easy to start out way too fast.
Getting caught up in the excitement early on in a race is natural, and “it’s easy to let that excitement dictate your pace,” says Reznik. If there’s any decline in the opening sections of your marathon (like the second mile of the NYC Marathon), it tends to be that much more difficult to restrain yourself and settle into a controlled rhythm.
How to prep:
Plan to begin slightly slower than your goal pace, advises Wilpers, and allow yourself to warm up when you’re in the race rather than forcing the pace from the beginning. “From there, the goal is to gradually settle into a rhythm and put yourself in a position to finish strong,” he says.

Ann Chisholm, owner and coach at Tropos Fitness Club in Victoria, British Columbia, stands before a crowd of about 20 women huddling in a circle under an outdoor tent, eager to learn about strength training despite the rainy weather.
“What are three common weaknesses in endurance athletes I see in the gym?” she asks them.
The group shouts out guesses. The first two are easy. Glutes! Adductors!—Chisholm agrees.
What’s the third one? Hip flexors? They’re up there, but there is something more important, Chisholm says.
This is the last session on the last day of FeistyFest, a three-day movement and educational festival for women held in September in Breinigsville, Pennsylvania, and none of the previous groups guessed the third one correctly, Chisholm says, before revealing the answer: “Power explosiveness!”
You can think of your explosive power as those first couple of seconds of your movement, the initial burst, Chisholm says. You’re recruiting fast-twitch muscle fibers, which quickly contract and generate high force, and activating your nervous system, which fires signals to your muscles at a high speed to help you coordinate complex movements.
“Injuries don’t happen when you’re just simply running forward often,” Chisholm says. When she sees them happen most? While moving laterally—“when you have to move quickly or in a different direction.” And that’s where explosive power comes in to help.
When you run, your body absorbs two to three times your body weight, which puts a lot of pressure on your joints and ligaments. Explosive power helps you control those forces safely and efficiently, while also improving speed, stride efficiency, and joint resilience.
Let’s start with the bad news: a 47-year Swedish study from 2025 published in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle concluded that explosive power peaks in women at 19 and in men at 27. That’s when your body starts losing its first line of defense against sudden physical stressors, and you become more injury-prone.
The good news? “We can train that, so your body is prepared to absorb the impact,” Chisholm says.

T-Bills Yield Up to 4.45%. Why Would Retirees Choose Dividend Stocks?
Treasury bills are paying rates that beat several household-name dividend stocks right now, but the retiree who chases that yield without reading the fine print may find their income cut in half before the decade ends.
As of October 23, 2026, Treasury bills paid average yields of 4% on the 4-week bill, 4.17% on the 13-week, 4.35% on the 26-week, and 4.45% on the 52-week. Every one of those rates is higher than the published dividend yields on three of the long-tenured income stocks in this comparison. Even so, a higher starting yield says only part of the story for a retiree who needs income for the next 20 years.
How a Treasury Bill Pays, and Why Your Rate Resets at Every Rollover
A Treasury bill is a short-term loan to the U.S. government. The Treasury sells bills at a discount or at par (face value), and when the bill matures, you receive the full face value. The difference between what you pay and what you get back is your interest. TreasuryDirect explains that for bills, “interest” is the difference between what you paid and the face value you get when the bill matures. Bills pay nothing along the way. You collect everything when the bill matures.
Bills come in 4-, 6-, 8-, 13-, 17-, 26-, and 52-week terms, with a $100 minimum purchase. The 4-week through 26-week bills auction weekly, and the 52-week bill auctions every four weeks. Your rate is fixed at auction and stays fixed only until the bill matures. When it does, you get your principal back and have to buy a new bill at whatever rate the next auction sets. That is reinvestment risk, and for retirees who live on rolling bills, it is the main risk they carry.
Rates have already moved in both directions within a year. The Federal Reserve’s target range tops out at 4.00% as of October 25, 2026. It was 4.25% a year earlier, fell to 3.75% from December 10, 2025 through September 15, 2026, and returned to 4% on September 16, 2026. Bill yields move with it.
The 52-week yield was 4.49% on October 14 and 4.45% on October 23. Someone rolling 4-week bills will get a new rate about a dozen times a year. Someone holding a 52-week bill locks in one rate for the year and carries all the rollover risk at a single date.
Government backing has limits that retirees should understand. The full faith and credit of the United States backs payment at face value at maturity. It does not protect the market price if you sell it before it matures. If rates rise after you buy, you can sell early for less than you paid. That price risk is small on a 4-week bill and increases with longer maturities.
Treasury notes, the longer-dated version, pay a fixed coupon for years and swing more in price. Treasuries are also securities, so FDIC deposit insurance doesn’t apply. And government backing does nothing for buying power. Consumer prices rose 0.6% from August in the September 2026 CPI reading. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ research index for Americans 62 and older rose 0.5% over the same month.

Salesforce has told customers it will soon charge for every call an agent makes to its platform, and for anyone trying to forecast what that costs, the newest row on the company's rate card – the one that will meter external agent calls – reads "TBA."
In a document published September 17, 2026, Salesforce set a November target for a new billing model under its Headless Toolkit. The mechanic is plain: every successful call a registered agent makes to Salesforce, whether it arrives over Model Context Protocol (MCP) or a direct API, is metered as one Headless Platform Interaction (HPI) and tracked through the company's Digital Wallet.
Worth stating plainly: agentic usage is not metered today. Private plaintiffs’ lawyers stand to collect up to $1.27 billion from New Mexico if the state’s $25 billion court win against Meta Platforms this week is upheld, according to a Reuters review of a contract with the state.
New Mexico hired Chicago-based law firm DiCello Levitt to represent it in the Meta case, which alleged the tech company duped its users about who had access to their personal data on its Facebook platform.
The state’s 2025 contract with DiCello Levitt, reviewed by Reuters after a records request, says the firm can ask the judge overseeing the case to award it 20% of the first $50 million of any eventual recovery, 15% of the next $50 million, 10% of the next $150 million and 5% of any amounts over $250 million.
Related: Meta to Pay Historic $25 Billion in New Mexico Deception Case
New Mexico and other states have turned to private law firms in a growing number of cases against major technology companies to buttress their legal teams against deep-pocketed defendants. The outside lawyers typically don’t charge by the hour but are entitled to a cut of any winnings.
In the Meta case, a jury sided with the state in September, and a judge on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25 billion. Meta denied wrongdoing and said it will appeal. Legal experts including Villanova University law professor Peter Ormerod told Reuters this week that the company has a strong basis for arguing that the judgment should be reduced.
If New Mexico ultimately recovers $25 billion from Meta, DiCello Levitt’s fees could reach $1.27 billion under the law firm’s contract. The amount would come out of the funds Meta pays to New Mexico.
Uncertainty Over Final Payout
To be sure, Meta could win its appeal or the judgment could be trimmed, and the court is not obligated to award the firm the maximum fees allowed under its contract.
DiCello Levitt declined to comment about its fees. New Mexico’s lead lawyer at the firm, Corban Rhodes, in a statement called the court’s decision a “defining moment for consumer protection and privacy.”
Randi McGinn, a New Mexico lawyer who worked with the DiCello firm in representing the state, told Reuters her small Albuquerque firm is entitled to collect about 33% of its fees. DiCello’s contract allowed the firm to designate other lawyers as subcontractors.
McGinn, who delivered the state’s opening statement and closing argument, cautioned that a final outcome in the case could take several years.
“People will say it’s a lot of money. But the truth is, we won’t see any of that money unless we win an appeal,” McGinn said.
Contingency fee awards over $1 billion are exceedingly rare, said Fordham University law professor Howard Erichson. While New Mexico’s contract caps fees for DiCello Levitt near 5%, “the sheer size of the recovery means it could result in a massive fee here, so I would expect the court to examine it carefully,” Erichson said.
The New Mexico attorney general’s office and a Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the legal fees.
States Turn to Private Firms
Some companies and business groups say that giving private lawyers a stake in state enforcement actions can put lawyers’ financial interests in conflict with public policy concerns. Defenders of the practice counter that it helps level the playing field for states going up against companies that can afford armies of lawyers.

Exxon Mobil Corp. has lost its appeal of an $815.5 million compensatory damages judgment that was awarded to a Mobil gas station mechanic who developed leukemia after years of exposure to benzene in its gasoline.
On October 15, a three-judge panel of the Superior Court of Pennsylvania upheld the award, ruling in part that the oil giant’s challenges to the causation evidence and other issues in its appeal should have been but were not raised at trial.
The Superior Court panel also rejected Exxon’s claims that the award should be invalidated because it was “shockingly excessive and against the weight of the evidence.”
Plaintiff Paul Gill was exposed to benzene while working as a mechanic and gas attendant at an ExxonMobil service station in Potter County from 1974 to 1979. As part of his work, Gill used ExxonMobil gasoline to clean automobile parts, which was a common practice at the time. He did not wear gloves or other protective equipment because he did not know that he could be exposed to benzene in gasoline through inhalation and skin contact. Gill was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia years later in 2019.
He maintained that his exposure to Exxon’s gasoline some 40 years ago was a substantial factor contributing to the cause of his cancer and the leukemia has taken a “drastic toll” on his standard of living and his marriage. His complaint described a host of medical effects: He underwent blood transfusions and a stem-cell transplant; suffered loss of eye, liver, and skin function as well as chronic weakness, severe pain, depression and the stiffening of his joints and suffered from seizures and has gone into diabetic coma. Also, the cancer spread to his colon, liver and lungs. He has had to isolate himself from friends and family for fear that he will contract diseases from them.
Product Liability
Gill brought counts of negligence and product-defect strict liability against Exxon. In the May 2024 trial in the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas jurors heard evidence that ExxonMobil was aware decades ago that there is no safe level of benzene exposure and that Exxon failed to warn Gill of this dangerous and potentially lethal defect in its product, even though “the American Petroleum Institute advised its members, including ExxonMobil, that there was no safe level of benzene exposure in 1948.”
Exxon’s defense argued in part that Gill and his medical experts failed to prove that the gasoline caused his cancer. The oil giant maintained that instead of focusing on the gasoline product for which Exxon was sued, the plaintiff’s witnesses focused on benzene which is a separate and distinct product.
The jury sided with Gill. Jurists found that Exxon was negligent, that its gasoline was defectively designed, and that it had failed to warn about the known dangers of exposure to benzene in its gasoline.

Investing.com -- BofA Securities upgraded miner Anglo American to "buy" rating, saying value has re-emerged after a pullback and a proposed merger with Teck would create a copper-focused company.
BofA set a price objective of 4,700 pence per share, based on 1x its sum-of-the-parts valuation, which adds up the value of each business. It assumes the Teck merger proceeds and includes risked values for near-term corporate and procurement synergies and longer-term ones at Collahuasi and Quebrada Blanca.
On a combined basis, BofA estimates the shares would trade at less than 7 times 2027 and 2028 estimated enterprise value to EBITDA, versus 8 to 15 times for copper peers.
The companies expect the merger to close by March 2027, subject to China anti-trust approval, which BofA called a key risk. Anglo and Teck have engaged with Chinese authorities and said talks are proceeding "as expected".
Reuters has reported that a multi-year offtake agreement could be enough to ease China's anti-trust concerns. BofA said forced asset disposals would make completing the deal more challenging.
BofA models near-term combined copper production of about 945,000 tonnes a year. Collahuasi in Chile, 44% owned by Anglo, is about 570,000 tonnes a year and one of the world's largest copper mines.
Adding QBII, about 240,000 tonnes a year and 60% owned by Teck, plus 175,000 tonnes a year of volume upside from operational synergies, could take the combined site to about 1 million tonnes a year, with Anglo Teck's equity share about 50%.
Other assets include Quellaveco in Peru (300,000 tonnes a year, 60% Anglo), Los Bronces in Chile (175,000 tonnes, 50% Anglo), Antamina in Peru (400,000 tonnes copper equivalent, 22.5% Teck) and Highland Valley in Canada (120,000 tonnes, 100% Teck).
Anglo is shedding non-core assets: coking coal and nickel sales are agreed, though nickel remains subject to anti-trust approval, while the De Beers diamonds sale is ongoing and challenged by pricing. BofA said it does not think any of these would derail perception of value in the combined company.

Coke and Philip Morris both beat expectations this quarter, but each is quietly betting against its own best product to survive the next decade. Which sacrifice looks smarter for your portfolio?
Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO | KO Price Prediction) and Philip Morris International (NYSE:PM) both beat expectations in their latest earnings reports. Both are old habits that are still changing. Coke sold more regular and zero-sugar soda during a World Cup summer. Philip Morris moved further into IQOS, ZYN and VEEV while cigarettes paid for the shift. Each generates strong cash flow through a different business model.
Coke Sold More Soda While Philip Morris Raised Cigarette Prices
Coke’s second-quarter unit case volume rose 5%. Trademark Coca-Cola had its strongest volume growth in 17 years, not counting the COVID rebound, so demand for the flagship drink remains strong. Coca-Cola Zero Sugar grew 16%, which makes it the main low-sugar growth driver. CEO Henrique Braun described the goal this way: “Our mission is simple, ensuring our brands are valued, relevant and worth choosing.”
At Philip Morris, third-quarter combustible pricing rose 8.9% even though cigarette shipments were flat. Marlboro can still raise prices without losing smokers. Smoke-free products now make up over 40% of net revenues. ZYN’s share of the pouch category rose 1.4 points from June to September, which shows ZYN gained ground against rivals.
Coke Spends on Affordability While Philip Morris Gives Up Margin for ZYN
Coke is putting money into keeping drinks affordable. Asia Pacific price/mix fell 9% while volume in the region grew 8%. Coke is giving up margin now to win future customers in India and China. Net leverage of 1.4x EBITDA is below Coke’s target range, so the balance sheet has room to spare.
Philip Morris is taking a bigger hit on purpose. ZYN cans are moving to 20 pouches at the old 15-pouch price, which works out to “approximately 25% less revenue per pouch.” Fourth-quarter U.S. operating income should come in “around zero or slightly negative.” That is a big short-term sacrifice. Even so, the company raised its dividend 8.8% to $1.60 a quarter.

Management expects revenue to lag for “three quarters.” Rising excise taxes in Japan and Germany add more uncertainty. For Coke, you should keep an eye on the redesigned Coca-Cola Zero Zero aimed at evening occasions. The fourth quarter will also have six fewer days than last year, and Coke’s tax case against the IRS is still waiting on an appeals court ruling.
Why Coke Fits My Low-Stress Portfolio Better
I prefer Coke for stability. It has raised its dividend for 63 years in a row and guides to about $12.4B of free cash flow. My worry is valuation. Shares are up 35.2% this year at about 30 times earnings, so a lot of good news is already priced in.
Philip Morris pairs a strong income profile with higher regulatory risk. Its $6.40 annual payout is backed by Marlboro’s pricing power. If U.S. ZYN profits recover by mid-2027, I would like Philip Morris a lot more.

Asked last month during a stop in St. Peters, Kehoe said he intends to run in 2028 “if Missourians will have us again.”
He faced the question again days later and told Nexstar the decision was a family one.
“We thought about it,” he said. “We prayed about it.”
On former House Speaker Elijah Haahr’s radio show, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick was asked whether he’d run for governor if Kehoe didn’t. Fitzpatrick said he’d consider it, then emphasized that Kehoe has been “very clear both in public and in private settings” that he’s running.
Kehoe has been consistent and clear. So why does everyone keep asking?
Part of the answer is Andrew Bailey.
The former attorney general returned to Missouri after a reportedly rough year at the FBI and almost immediately began sounding like a candidate. His allied PAC has more than half a million dollars in the bank. He has talked with people in Missouri politics about the governor’s office.
When Haahr asked whether any statewide Republican deserves a primary challenge, Bailey didn’t say no. He said to give him a year at home “and let’s have that conversation.” Then last week, Bailey publicly criticized the decision to give St. Louis’ police chief a substantial raise. The board that approved it is dominated by Kehoe appointees.
Asked by reporters whether he could beat Bailey in a primary, Kehoe said: “I’m not thinking about running against Andrew.”
But Bailey didn’t create all the questions about Kehoe’s future. Those were already circulating.
Andrew Bailey is back in Missouri and talking like a candidate
Kehoe has been remarkably effective at getting a fractious Republican legislature to do what he wants. He persuaded lawmakers to approve a massive incentive package to keep the Chiefs and Royals in Missouri. He secured votes for his tax agenda, helped push through a gerrymandered congressional map and has put his stamp on the state’s education leadership.
The trouble is what happened after lawmakers said yes.
The Chiefs are moving to Kansas.
In August, voters overwhelmingly rejected Amendment 5, which would have put Missouri on a path toward eliminating its income tax. Amendment 4, the effort to rewrite the rules for citizen initiatives, lost badly alongside it.
The congressional map Kehoe signed into law won’t be used Nov. 3, either. A successful referendum effort and a string of court rulings derailed Republican hopes of capturing seven of Missouri’s eight congressional seats this year.
Along the way, Kehoe’s approval rating slipped underwater in the SLU/YouGov poll: 40% approving, 49% disapproving.

Missouri to raise speed limit to 75 mph on stretches of four interstates
(photo courtesy of the Missouri Department of Transportation)
Missourians will soon be able to drive a bit faster on some rural roads.
The Missouri Department of Transportation has selected portions of four interstates where drivers can go 75 mph, rather than the typical 70 mph.
MoDOT crews will work to update all speed limit signs in these areas this fall and ask that all drivers abide by the posted speed limit signs in these areas, according to a MoDOT news release.
The speed limit will not be raised until a new sign is posted.
This comes after a new law permitting the department to raise the maximum rural highway speed limit to 75 mph. Senate Bill 1408 was passed on May 15, and Gov. Mike Kehoe signed it into law on July 13.
Each location was reviewed through a detailed process to determine if the location was eligible for a raised speed limit.
Each review looked at current traffic volumes, truck traffic volumes, current speed data, crash history, terrain, road design, the presence of safety countermeasures, existing speed limits of border states in areas near state lines and active construction, according to the news release.
Portions of I-29, I-35, I-49 and I-55 will raise the maximum speed limit. Eight sections of these interstates will have raised limits, according to the release:
- A 64-mile stretch of I-29 in Andrew County from Exit 56 to approximately 2.5 miles south of the Iowa border
- A 55-mile stretch of I-35 from the northern Cameron city limit to approximately four miles south of the Iowa border
- A 24-mile stretch of I-49 from the Arkansas border to Exit 24
- A 45-mile stretch of I-49 from Exit 56 to just south of Exit 101 in Nevada
- A 17-mile stretch of I-55 from the Arkansas border to mile marker 16.6 just south of the I-55 interchange
- A 45-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 19.8 just north of the MO 84 interchange to mile marker 64.9 at the Route AA bridge
- A 16-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 70.5 just north of the Route HH interchange to mile marker 86.6 just south of the Route PP interchange
- A 59-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 106.4 just north of Exit 105 to mile marker 164.9 at the Jefferson County line
MoDOT said it will monitor and evaluate crash data in these areas and, if needed, will bring the maximum speed limit back down to 70 mph.
“An increased speed limit may allow motorists to reach their destinations faster, but safety must remain a priority,” Missouri State Highway Patrol Col. Michael Turner said.
“The Patrol and our traffic safety partners at MoDOT remain committed to reducing the number and severity of traffic crashes in Missouri. It is each driver’s responsibility to make safe decisions while driving.”

The United Arab Emirates shut more beaches after an oil spill in the Persian Gulf raised concerns over environmental and health impacts.
Sharjah said Al Hamriya Beach has been closed as a precautionary measure to prevent pollution from the oil spill. Ras Al Khaimah said that all its beaches are closed until further notice, without specifying the reason for the closure.
On Friday the UAE’s climate ministry detected the spill off the coast Umm Al Quwain, north of Dubai, and temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas in the emirate. It didn’t identify the tanker.
Odors in Umm Al Quwain, Sharjah and Ajman don’t pose health risks to residents, the ministry said in a post on X.
Specialized teams and relevant authorities were dispatched to Sharjah to undertake necessary measures to ensure the safety of beaches and prevent pollutants from reaching them, the emirate’s media office said.
The region has suffered oil spills and leaks in recent months. In August, a tanker ran aground near Oman’s southeastern coast leaving the country to battle a slick covering about six-and-a-half times the land area of Manhattan. Shortly after, Iran was dealing with an oil spill off Qeshm Island, near a breeding ground for endangered hawksbill sea turtles.
Conflict in the region is also increasing the risk of oil spills and maritime pollution.
A cargo vessel sank in the Strait of Hormuz this month after a strike that sparked a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Freighters struck by projectiles can leak ship fuel, even if the main oil storage tanks aren’t breached, endangering wildlife and marine environments.

Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.
GMO Internet Group, a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorized access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive 5,000 yen ($32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday.
“The internet itself is now starting to break down,” said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading.
Shares of GMO, which had a market value of $2.6 billion as of Friday’s close, slumped almost 16% on Monday to a four-month low against a 0.2% rise in Tokyo’s benchmark index .TOPX.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government planned to compile an emergency package of measures against cyberattacks by next week.
The government said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organizations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet.
More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks, with industry experts saying AI is helping automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.
“The internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people,” said Kumagai.
Government and company websites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts.
Call on Japan to Step Up Cyberdefense
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply defense measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefence system this month.
The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralize threats.
“Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan,” wrote Kumagai.
GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply. In an update on Monday to his blog post, Kumagai said that the party had demanded $50 million in cryptocurrency.
GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws.
The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses.
White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote.

Rising prices squeeze more Americans ahead of pivotal midterm elections
General Manager Brian Horak walks down an aisle at Post 60 Market in Emerson, Nebraska. A new national report shows how everyday costs have increased for Americans (Kevin Hardy/Stateline).
Americans’ growing frustration over high prices has defined many political campaigns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Rising costs of healthcare, gas and groceries during President Donald Trump’s second term have put Republicans on defense, not only in Washington, but in statehouse and gubernatorial races across the country.
As the political environment continues to sour for Republicans, a new analysis released by the Urban Institute on Monday underscores just how expensive everyday life has become in America: Gas and electricity prices are rising much faster than paychecks. Housing, childcare and healthcare are becoming a bigger strain for millions of people.
And affordability pressure is worsening in once-affordable havens such as Atlanta; Louisville, Kentucky; and Rochester, New York, where costs of housing, groceries and healthcare are increasing faster than the national average.
The latest installment of The American Affordability Tracker from the left-leaning think tank details how costs of food, housing, energy and healthcare have changed across all 50 states over recent years. High prices are pinching people across income brackets, with an estimated 49% of families unable to afford the basic costs of living. That’s according to Urban Institute’s true cost of economic security calculation, which measures how much is needed to live securely.
“We’re not saying that 49% of people are poor. We’re saying that they’re not secure,” said Gregory Acs, an Urban Institute fellow who worked on the research project. “Even if they’re paying all their bills, they’re paying all their bills at best.”
He said the analysis confirms that the economic angst so many people feel is justified — despite strong national economic indicators such as low unemployment and growing gross domestic product.
“They are not crazy. They’re not making it up,” Acs said. “They’re not being marketed into feeling bad. They really do have struggles.”
Among other findings, the report shows that average annual childcare costs for two young children have risen $6,600 over the past decade. Since January 2025, gas prices have risen by 33% — an average increase of $1.02 per gallon nationally. And premiums for benchmark plans on the Affordable Care Act Marketplace are up 22% since last year, now averaging $611 per month.
Affordability politics
Those struggles have become a political liability for Republicans, who control the White House, both chambers of Congress, most state legislatures and a majority of governor’s offices.
All midterm elections, as a referendum on the sitting president, are difficult for incumbents in the majority. But this cycle is particularly charged because of Trump’s promises to improve the economy during his 2024 campaign, said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at The George Washington University.

Assicurazioni Generali SpA plans to reduce around 9% of its workforce in Germany and downsize locations as part of a simplification effort in the European country.
Generali plans to set up five regional centers in Munich, Cologne, Karlsruhe, Hamburg and Saarbrücken, bringing together teams currently spread across Germany to reduce costs and strengthen collaboration, the Italian company said in a statement on Friday. The job reductions will mainly be achieved through “voluntary retirement arrangements.”
The insurer will invest “a three-digit million euro amount” in IT, digitization and artificial intelligence. It also plans to recruit new employees “with skills for the future.”
The planned job cuts are part of Generali’s broader push to streamline its operations and direct resources toward areas offering stronger growth and profitability. Under Chief Executive Officer Philippe Donnet’s strategy through 2027, Italy’s biggest insurer is seeking to accelerate growth in its preferred profit pools while simplifying its operating model, increasing automation and improving productivity.
In Germany, the company has already been cutting costs and modernizing its operations, with a target to reduce its cost-income ratio to 52% by 2027, from 57% in 2024. Generali had more than 9,000 employees in the country, where last year it generated over €15 billion ($16.8 billion) of premium income, according to its website.
The news was first reported by German outlet Manager Magazin.

The Permian Lever Exxon Controls
At Barclays’ energy conference on September 9, Chief Financial Officer Neil Hansen said of the Pioneer acquisition: “we anticipated achieving about $2 billion a year of synergies, and we’ve been able to double that.” Permian output hit a record of more than 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels a day in the second quarter, according to Exxon’s July 31 results.
The bigger lever is recovery. Hansen said only a fairly small share of the Permian’s oil in place is being recovered, and described doubling Permian recovery as what he called a stated objective, pursued through 40 complementary technologies across primary and secondary recovery. Some, he said, “will produce the same amount of volume, but with fewer wells.” Fewer wells per barrel means less capital per barrel, a cost gain Exxon controls whatever crude does. Doubling recovery is an objective, not a result, and Hansen gave no date for it.

On October 22, the Financial Times reported that Infineum, the fuel and lubricant additives maker Exxon owns 50:50 with Shell (SHEL), has hired Bank of America to explore a sale at about $8 billion. The FT framed it as part of Shell’s push to shed chemicals assets, said the process is early and may not produce a deal, and Reuters could not verify the report. Exxon’s half would be roughly $4 billion of that valuation, about 0.5% of its $753 billion market value.
A sale would fit the pattern Hansen described, saying “a lot of” Exxon’s structural savings so far have come from divestments. He expects future savings to come “more and more from the organization we’ve designed.”
